summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey measured AI use among construction firms at 14.3 percent in its most recent reading, down slightly from 14.9 percent in the prior period. These figures come from firms answering directly whether they used AI in the preceding two weeks, making this one of the few hard adoption counts available for the sector rather than an estimate drawn from surveys of intent or aspiration.

The Associated General Contractors of America, which represents over 27,000 member firms, tracks technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across American builders, and its survey data serves as the principal adoption record for the contractor community. AGC has organized programming specifically around practical AI applications, convening construction leaders, technology experts, and AI innovators to work through what implementation actually looks like at the project and enterprise levels, a framing that suggests the conversation has moved past awareness into operational questions.

BuiltWorlds, which describes itself as a global network for buildings and infrastructure professionals, runs the sector's dedicated intelligence function on this topic. Its annual AI and machine learning conference covers use cases spanning the full construction and building process, including site robotics, jobsite sensor networks, and digital preconstruction, and its member benchmarking program tracks how companies are deploying specific solutions and what lessons they draw from those deployments. The network's 2026 conference agenda specifically highlights what it calls practical power and quick wins, language that points to a current emphasis on demonstrable near-term returns rather than longer-horizon transformation.

On the capital side, CREtech and MetaProp track venture investment flowing into architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside the broader property technology market, offering a view of where private funding concentrates within this space. The sourced material does not specify particular dollar figures or deal counts, so the precise shape of that investment flow is not detailed here.

For a firm weighing deployment, the Census figure confirms that roughly one in seven construction businesses is already using AI in some active capacity, and the slight quarter-on-quarter dip from 14.9 to 14.3 percent is small enough that it does not suggest retreat. The institutional infrastructure around adoption, through AGC's member programs and BuiltWorlds' research and conference activity, is more developed than in many comparable industries, which means operators looking to learn from peers have more structured venues to do so than the overall adoption rate alone might imply. The sourced material does not address regulatory posture or documented ROI figures, so those dimensions remain open questions for any buyer conducting due diligence.
